headline: In Tennessee, $10 million went after the independent, and Blackburn barely won
dek: Committees backing Marsha Blackburn spent close to $10 million attacking David Hatley, a self-funded independent. Blackburn then beat Democrat Jerri Green by 2.5 points, even though Green's campaign could barely afford TV ads.
summary: Pro-Blackburn PACs spent about $10 million against an independent, and Blackburn beat an underfunded Democrat by 2.5 points.

paras.text: Most of the outside money in Tennessee's race for governor paid for one message: that David Hatley, an independent businessman from upper East Tennessee, should not be governor. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican U.S. senator, won on Nov. 3 with 955,298 votes to 902,615 for Democrat Jerri Green, according to AP results published by The New York Times. That is a 2.5-point margin in a state President Trump carried by 29.7 points in 2024. Hatley took 9.3% of the vote, according to the secretary of state's unofficial count.

The Federal Election Commission data The Watch had for this story showed no outside spending in Tennessee's federal races. In the Senate race, Bill Hagerty, the Republican incumbent, beat Marquita Bradshaw by 12.2 points. Hagerty raised more than $13 million this cycle, according to the FEC, and Bradshaw raised about $38,000, the Nashville Banner reported.

Blackburn ran with help from two state political action committees. The first, Team Tennessee, was established in 2025 to boost Blackburn. Its donors included TikTok investor Jeff Yass, who gave $1 million, as well as tobacco company Reynolds American ($100,000) and CoreCivic ($100,000 combined from the company and its former CEO). The prediction-market company Kalshi, which had recently lost a court fight with the state, donated $50,000 to Team Tennessee.

The second, the Tennessee Freedom Fund, is registered to the same Washington, D.C., address as Club for Growth Action and has the same officers, led by Club for Growth CEO David McIntosh. Club for Growth is a national conservative group that backs private-school vouchers. Part of the Fund's money traces back to Blackburn's own federal account. Marsha for Senate contributed $4.8 million to the Club for Growth Action super PAC on May 8, and the School Freedom Fund, a related committee funded by Yass, gave $4.81 million to the Tennessee Freedom Fund between May 7 and July 7. Tennessee law does not let Blackburn spend her U.S. Senate money directly on a state race. Since 2023, School Freedom Fund has raised around $30 million, $27 million of it from Yass. By August the two pro-Blackburn PACs had consolidated under one entity after raising a total of $12 million. That total included $250,000 each from Anthropic and Advance Financial, a payday lender, in the pre-primary period.

The third committee, Choose Freedom PAC, registered in Tennessee on Sept. 18, took a $4.2 million donation that same day, and spent the same amount attacking Hatley. It took in another $2.3 million on Oct. 13 and spent it the same day. All of its money came from Choose Freedom Inc., a Massachusetts-based dark-money group. "Dark money" here is the legal term: a nonprofit that does not have to disclose its donors. According to The New York Times, Choose Freedom Inc. has spent $22 million in U.S. House and Senate races. The PAC's Alabama address is shared by the Crosby Ottenhoff Group, a political accounting and compliance firm. The Tennessee Lookout described the group as linked to MAGA Inc.

The other two candidates raised far less from donors. Green raised $995,496.69 in the third quarter and more than $1.5 million over her whole run. Hatley paid for his campaign himself; he has put in $12 million of his own money and spent more than $5 million, mostly on TV and social media ads.

The ad war started in the Republican primary. The Tennessee Freedom Fund ran one video echoing President Donald Trump's praise for Blackburn, even though Trump had not endorsed anyone in that race. Against U.S. Rep. John Rose, her primary rival, it spent nearly $5 million on TV ads and mailers. Blackburn was also attacked. The American Exceptionalism Institute, a 501(c)(4) nonprofit, ran an AI-generated spoof of a pharmaceutical ad calling her "queen pharma mama." After her lawyers objected, Comcast and Viamedia pulled the ad. The state Registry of Election Finance referred the complaint to Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti.

After the primary, the target became Hatley. Blackburn's campaign paid for a website called DeadbeatDave.com. In Choose Freedom's TV ad, a man in an orange jumpsuit kicks his feet up on a desk while a narrator brings up Hatley's 1998 bank-fraud conviction. The ad and website also point to $7.7 million in tax liens. Hatley has addressed both publicly and in a book. In total, the attack ads against Hatley were funded by the Tennessee Freedom Fund ($3 million) and Choose Freedom ($6.5 million).

Green's campaign had little money for ads. In the third quarter it spent $67,101.97 on advertising, including $19,226.75 on TV ads and $9,805.12 on social media. In a post-election column, the Lookout's Sam Stockard wrote that TV viewers saw a barrage of anti-Hatley ads and a few Blackburn spots with former swimmer Riley Gaines about transgender athletes, and hardly anything about Green.

The side that spent the most won, but only narrowly and with less than a majority of the vote. Hatley rose in the polls on a self-funded October ad push, with some polls showing him between 10 and 20 percent. He finished at 9.3%. The campaign filings cannot show whether the attack ads caused that drop.

The Senate race on the same ballot gives a point of comparison. Hagerty had no outside spending in The Watch's FEC data and won by 12.2 points. Blackburn's margin was 9.7 points smaller. In Stockard's view, Blackburn depended on dark-money groups to attack Hatley and refused to debate, and was fortunate that the Democratic Party never really got behind Green or spent heavily to elect her. That is commentary, not a finding. In her concession, Green said "This was just one battle for our state and it was not the end of the fight."
